proposals.relationship: In their 1982 preface, Stedman Jones and Raphael Samuel credit Hobsbawm with opening the questions about social being, culture and politics that their collection takes forward.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint authorial acknowledgment, not sole testimony by Stedman Jones or formal supervision. The preface recognizes strengths and limits of base–superstructure explanation. Original 1982 text read in the publisher’s 2016 reprint preview; individual contributions unread.
primary_locators: Preface ix–x, especially p. x final two paragraphs; PDF pages 12–13 (one-based).

proposals.relationship: Reviewing Labouring Men in 1965, Stedman Jones challenges Hobsbawm’s dismissal of Fabian influence and warns against reducing an intellectual tradition’s significance to its sociological roots.
proposals.evidence_note: The signed review also praises Hobsbawm’s craft studies and recovery of working-class politics. This is a specific disagreement within a positive review, not rejection of his historical achievement; Hobsbawm’s book not freshly read.
primary_locators: Publisher HTML paragraphs beginning “Nevertheless they were the fountainhead” and “On that criterion”; opening and final praise checked. No print-page locator invented.

proposals.relationship: Palmer argues that Stedman Jones’s reading of Chartist rhetoric separates language and politics too sharply from the material contexts in which class consciousness could develop (1993).
proposals.evidence_note: Palmer calls the rhetorical reading insightful but limited. His own explanation retains the state’s relative autonomy while making material relations constrain political language. This fresh 1993 argument does not silently upgrade the unread Descent into Discourse (1990).
primary_locators: IRSH 38 (1993), printed 143–146, especially 143 third paragraph and 145 second paragraph; PDF pages 11–14.

proposals.relationship: Eley and Keith Nield defend the gains of Languages of Class but criticize Stedman Jones for narrowing linguistic analysis to published Chartist rhetoric and excluding the social archive (2000).
proposals.evidence_note: Keith Nield retains equal authorial credit. Their critique accepts much of the political reinterpretation of Chartism; it challenges the restricted archive and oversynthesized public language, not linguistic analysis itself. Mixed critic edge 1159 remains unchanged.
primary_locators: Farewell to the Working Class?, printed 6–8, especially 7; footnotes 17–21, printed 26–27.

proposals.relationship: Lawrence explicitly acknowledges Stedman Jones, his supervisor in the 1980s, as an enduring intellectual inspiration in Speaking for the People (1998).
proposals.evidence_note: Lawrence’s own acknowledgments establish the mentoring debt. They also credit Miles Taylor, Jane Elliott and other readers; this does not assign the book’s arguments solely to his supervisor or settle the separate 1993 joint reply.
primary_locators: Speaking for the People, acknowledgments xi–xii, final sentence of first paragraph on xii.

proposals.relationship: As Paulo Fontes reconstructs her 1987 review, Dorothy Thompson criticizes Stedman Jones’s narrow corpus of Chartist political language and rejects separating the movement’s political character from its class setting.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated through Fontes (1999), pp. 103–105, with Palmer’s independent acknowledgment (1993), p. 143. She calls for wider verbal, nonverbal and archival evidence. Her 1987 review and later collected versions remain unread here; Dorothy is distinct from E. P. Thompson.
primary_locators: Fontes (1999), printed pp. 103–105: restriction of language corpus, wider sources and political/social distinction; quotes attributed by Fontes to Thompson (1987), pp. 56–57.
Palmer (1993), printed p. 143, paragraph explicitly crediting Dorothy Thompson’s Political Thought objection.

proposals.relationship: Wood challenges Stedman Jones’s move from rejecting a simple correspondence between class and politics to declaring Chartist politics autonomous; inherited radical language can be transformed by capitalist class relations.
proposals.evidence_note: The Retreat from Class (1986) is read only in selected primary text from a third-party transcription of the revised 1998 edition, pp. 102–107. Wood distinguishes his substantial historical research from abstract theory and targets its theoretical conclusions. Her 1995 discussion is separately checked in the publisher’s 2010 German translation, pp. 79–80; translators Ingrid Scherf and Christoph Jünke retain credit. Neither whole book is claimed read.
primary_locators: The Retreat from Class, revised 1998 edition, chapter 7, pp. 102–107, especially 103–105; 1986 original publication remains distinct.

Demokratie contra Kapitalismus (2010 German translation of Democracy against Capitalism, 1995), pp. 79–80 and note 31, including its distinction between the shorter 1982 essay and the 1983 self-interpretation.
